YieldSpace in Lean

A walk through a Lean 4 proof of eight properties of the constant power sum invariant

Lean 4 and Mathlib · October 2026 · A companion to Niemerg, Robinson and Livnev, YieldSpace: An Automated Liquidity Provider for Fixed Yield Tokens (2020) · Source on GitHub

Abstract

YieldSpace is a formula for pools that trade a fixed yield token (a fyToken) against the asset it pays out at maturity. Its invariant, x1−t+y1−t=k, includes the time to maturity t, and it makes the interest rate offered by the pool a simple function of the pool's reserves. This page walks through a machine-checked proof, written in Lean 4 with the Mathlib library, of eight properties of the pool's trades. Rates are non-negative when the pool holds at least as much fyToken as base. Every trade has exactly one outcome. Buying raises the price and selling lowers it. Splitting a trade into pieces changes nothing. A round trip loses money when there is a fee. Larger trades get worse prices. Scaling the pool scales its trades. Trading becomes a one-for-one exchange at maturity. Each section states one property, proves it informally, and shows the statement that Lean checked. Writing the statements precisely enough for a proof checker turned up a few places where the paper needs a qualification. Section 6 lists them.

1Introduction

A fyToken is a token that can be redeemed for exactly one unit of a target asset, such as one Dai, on a fixed maturity date. Before that date it usually trades for less than one unit, and the discount is an interest rate. For example, if a fyDai that matures in one year costs 0.95 Dai, a buyer who holds it to maturity earns 1/0.95−1≈5.3% over the year.

Many token exchanges on Ethereum are automated market makers. An automated market maker is a contract that holds reserves of two tokens and trades with anyone. It has no order book. Instead, it accepts any trade that leaves its reserves satisfying a fixed equation, called the invariant, and so the invariant sets the price.

YieldSpace [1] is an invariant designed for fyTokens. The paper derives it, and argues for its properties in the usual informal way. This page checks a set of those properties with a proof assistant: a program that accepts a proof only if every step follows from earlier steps, from definitions, and in the end from the axioms of mathematics. We use Lean 4 [2] and Mathlib [3], Lean's library of formalized mathematics. Mathlib already contains the tools the proofs need: real powers, derivatives, convex functions, the mean value theorem, and limits.

Table 1 lists the eight properties. They are numbered in the order in which they were first written down, as a list of things the formalization should prove. The sections below take them in a different order, so that each proof can use the ones before it.

Table 1. The eight properties, where they are proved, and the main Lean theorem for each.

3Round trips break even without a fee and lose with one5.8Params.roundTrip_loss

The Lean listings are copied from the project's source files by the script that builds this page, so they are exactly what Lean checked.

Section 2 describes pools defined by an invariant, the constant power sum formula, and the paper's fees. Section 3 explains enough Lean to read the listings. Section 4 shows how the pool is written down in Lean. Section 5 proves the eight properties. Section 6 lists the places where the formalization and the paper differ.

2Background

2.1Pools defined by an invariant

A pool holds x units of one token and y units of another. A trader who sends Δ units of the second token into the pool receives some amount of the first. The pool chooses that amount so that the reserves after the trade satisfy the same equation as the reserves before it. That equation is the pool's invariant.

The best-known invariant is the constant product x⋅y=k used by Uniswap. For example, a pool with x=y=100 has k=10000. To take 10 units of y out of it, a trader must raise x to 10000/90=111.11, so the trade costs 11.11 units of x, or 1.111 per unit of y.

Very small trades reveal the price the pool currently offers. If a trade moves the y reserve by dy and the x reserve by dx, the price of the y token, measured in units of the x token, is

p=−dydx​.(1)

This is the marginal price. Geometrically it is the slope of the curve of possible reserves at the current point, with the sign changed. In the example above the marginal price is x/y=1, while the trade of 10 units paid 1.111 per unit. A real trade has a size, and its average price is worse than the marginal price. Section 5.7 makes that precise.

2.2The constant power sum invariant

In YieldSpace, x is the reserve of the base token, the asset that the fyToken pays out at maturity (for example Dai), and y is the reserve of the fyToken. The invariant is

x1−t+y1−t=k,(2)

where t is the time to maturity, scaled so that 0<t<1 before maturity. In the original deployment t=1 corresponded to four years. When t=0, (2) is the constant sum x+y=k, which trades one for one. As t approaches 1, (2) approaches the constant product (paper, Appendix D). Figure 1 shows curves between these two.

To find the price, differentiate (2) along the curve:

(1−t)x−tdx+(1−t)y−tdy=0.

By (1), the price of a fyToken in base is then

p=−dydx​=x−ty−t​=(yx​)t.(3)

A fyToken bought at price p and held to maturity turns p units of base into 1. The return over the time that remains is

p1​−1=(xy​)t−1.(4)

The paper describes the rate differently. It defines r by p=(1+r)−t: r is the rate per unit of t, compounded over the time t that remains. Combining this with (3) gives

r=xy​−1.(5)

This is the property the formula was designed to have. The rate is the ratio of the reserves minus one, whatever the time to maturity. Both (4) and (5) are positive exactly when y>x.

The paper reaches (2) in the opposite direction. It starts from the requirement (5), turns it into the differential equation −dx/dy=(x/y)t, and integrates (paper, §4 and Appendix C). Here we take (2) as given and only need its consequences (3) to (5).

For example, take x=100, y=110 and t=0.5 (two years, if t=1 is four years). The price of a fyToken is (100/110)0.5=0.9535. A buyer earns 4.88% over the two years to maturity, and the paper's rate is r=10% per four years. We use this pool, (x,y)=(100,110) with t=0.5, as a running example. With t=0.5 the exponent 1−t is 1/2 and the invariant reads x​+y​=k, so most of the numbers below can be checked by hand.

2.3Fees

The paper charges fees in terms of rates rather than prices (paper, §5). A trader who buys fyToken should receive a lower rate than the pool's marginal rate, and a trader who sells fyToken should pay a higher one. The paper does this by replacing t with gt for buys and with t/g for sells, where 0<g≤1 is a fee parameter and g=1 means no fee:

x1−gt+y1−gtx1−t/g+y1−t/g​=k=k​​(buying fyToken),(selling fyToken).​(6)

On the buying curve the marginal price is (x/y)gt. When x<y, the base x/y is less than 1, so the smaller exponent gt gives a higher price than t does, as a fee should. In the paper's example, x=100, y=110 and g=0.95, buyers receive a marginal rate of (110/100)0.95−1≈9.48% instead of 10%, and sellers pay (110/100)1/0.95−1≈10.55%. When x>y the comparison reverses, and the fee favors the trader. Section 5.8 comes back to this.

The selling exponent 1−t/g must stay positive, so with a fee we also need t<g (paper, footnote 4).

3Enough Lean to read this page

Lean is a programming language in which statements and proofs are both written as code. A Lean file contains definitions and theorems, and Lean accepts a theorem only after checking its proof. Here is the first theorem of the project:

YieldSpace/Rates.leanstatement and proof
/-- **Theorem 1.** If `y ≥ x` the fyToken price is at most 1. -/
theorem price_le_one {t x y : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) (hx : 0 < x) (hxy : x ≤ y) :
    price t x y ≤ 1 :=
  rpow_le_one (div_nonneg hx.le (hx.trans_le hxy).le)
    ((div_le_one (hx.trans_le hxy)).2 hxy) ht

It reads as follows.

  • theorem price_le_one gives the result a name, so that other proofs can use it.
  • {t x y : ℝ} introduces three real numbers. The curly braces make them implicit: a proof that uses this theorem does not pass them, because Lean can work them out from the hypotheses.
  • (ht : 0 ≤ t), (hx : 0 < x) and (hxy : x ≤ y) are hypotheses. Each has a name so that the proof can refer to it.
  • After the last colon comes the conclusion, price t x y ≤ 1.
  • After := comes the proof. This one is a single expression. It applies Mathlib's lemma rpow_le_one, which says that be≤1 whenever 0≤b≤1 and 0≤e, to proofs of the three facts that lemma needs. div_nonneg proves 0≤x/y, and div_le_one turns x≤y into x/y≤1.

Longer proofs are written as a sequence of tactics after the word by. Each tactic transforms the goal, the statement that remains to be proved, until nothing is left. The proofs on this page mostly use the tactics in Table 2.

Table 2. Tactics used in the listings.
TacticWhat it does
unfold fReplaces f by its definition.
rw [h]Rewrites the goal with an equation h : a = b, replacing a by b.
have h : P := …Proves an intermediate fact P and names it h.
linarith, nlinarithClose the goal by linear (or simple nonlinear) arithmetic on the hypotheses.
exact eCloses the goal with a term e that proves it.
simp, field_simp, ringSimplify, clear denominators, or prove an identity of commutative rings.
obtain ⟨a, b⟩ := hSplits a hypothesis of the form “A and B” or “there exists” into its parts.
calcProves a chain of equalities and inequalities one link at a time.

Two details of Mathlib matter for this project.

Real powers. In Lean, x ^ a with a real exponent a is Mathlib's function Real.rpow. It is defined for every real x. For negative x, Mathlib sets xa=ealogxcos(aπ), where logx means log∣x∣. This choice is convenient for the library and has no meaning for reserves. So every statement on this page that takes a power carries hypotheses that keep the base non-negative, either directly or through a condition such as k−za≥0.

Checking for gaps. Lean lets a proof be left unfinished with the keyword sorry, and then accepts the statement anyway. The command #print axioms lists everything a theorem depends on in the end. For each of the project's main theorems the answer is [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], the three standard axioms that all of Mathlib uses. An unfinished proof anywhere in the chain would add sorryAx to that list. There are none.

4The model in Lean

4.1One exponent for every curve

The fee-free curve and the two fee curves in (6) have the same form, xa+ya=k, with

a=1−τ,τ∈{t, gt, t/g}.

In every case 0<τ<1, so 0<a<1. The project therefore proves almost every result once, for an arbitrary exponent a in (0,1), and then applies it to each curve. The invariant and its solution for one reserve are:

YieldSpace/Defs.leandefinitions
/-- The constant power sum `x ^ a + y ^ a` (paper eq. 1, with `a = 1 - t`). -/
def inv (a x y : ℝ) : ℝ := x ^ a + y ^ a

/-- Solve the invariant for one reserve: the `r ≥ 0` with `r ^ a + z ^ a = k`. -/
def solve (a k z : ℝ) : ℝ := (k - z ^ a) ^ a⁻¹

solve a k z is the reserve r that satisfies ra+za=k, namely

r=(k−za)1/a.(7)

Lean writes 1/a as a⁻¹. The formula only makes sense when k−za≥0, and the lemmas about solve assume this. The two basic lemmas say that solve does solve the invariant, and that it is the only non-negative solution:

YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement and proof
lemma solve_rpow (ha : 0 < a) {k z : ℝ} (h : 0 ≤ k - z ^ a) :
    solve a k z ^ a = k - z ^ a :=
  rpow_inv_rpow h ha.ne'

/-- Uniqueness: a non-negative reserve that satisfies the invariant is `solve`. -/
lemma eq_solve (ha : 0 < a) {r k z : ℝ} (hr : 0 ≤ r) (h : inv a r z = k) :
    r = solve a k z := by
  rw [solve, ← h, inv, add_sub_cancel_right, rpow_rpow_inv hr ha.ne']

The proof of eq_solve is a single chain of rewrites. If ra+za=k then k−za=ra, and (ra)1/a=r when r≥0, which is Mathlib's rpow_rpow_inv.

4.2Trades

A trader can specify a trade in two ways: by the amount sent in, or by the amount taken out. We call these trades with a fixed input and trades with a fixed output. Write the pool's reserves as (x,y), and let the trade change the y reserve by Δ.

  • In outGivenIn a x y Δ the trader sends Δ of the y token in and receives x−(k−(y+Δ)a)1/a.(8)
  • In inGivenOut a x y Δ the trader takes Δ of the y token out and pays (k−(y−Δ)a)1/a−x.(9)

In both, k=xa+ya is computed from the reserves just before the trade, as the paper specifies (§4.1).

YieldSpace/Defs.leandefinitions
/-- Trader sends `Δ` of Y in; this much X comes out. -/
def outGivenIn (a x y Δ : ℝ) : ℝ := x - solve a (inv a x y) (y + Δ)

/-- Trader takes `Δ` of Y out; this much X must go in. -/
def inGivenOut (a x y Δ : ℝ) : ℝ := solve a (inv a x y) (y - Δ) - x

For example, in the running pool k=100​+110​=20.488. A trader who sells 10 fyToken leaves the base reserve at (20.488−120​)2=90.890, and so receives 9.110 base, an average price of 0.911 per fyToken. That is less than the marginal price 0.9535. Section 5.7 shows that it always is.

4.3The four trades with fees

In the generic functions, y is whichever reserve the trader specifies. For trades with fees we always call the base reserve x and the fyToken reserve y, and each of the four possible trades uses the curve that matches its direction (Table 3).

Table 3. The four trades. Trades that buy fyToken use the exponent 1−gt; trades that sell fyToken use 1−t/g.
Lean nameTrader sendsTrader receivesExponentDefined as
sellFYTokenΔ fyTokenbase1−t/goutGivenIn aSell x y Δ
buyFYTokenbaseΔ fyToken1−gtinGivenOut aBuy x y Δ
sellBaseΔ basefyToken1−gtoutGivenIn aBuy y x Δ
buyBasefyTokenΔ base1−t/ginGivenOut aSell y x Δ

The paper describes fees only by direction, buying or selling fyToken. It does not say which curve a trade uses when the trader fixes the amount of base rather than the amount of fyToken. Table 3 uses the curve for the trade's direction in every case.

YieldSpace/Defs.leandefinitions
/-- Time to maturity `t` and fee parameter `g` (`g = 1` means no fee). The paper needs
`t / g < 1` so that the sell-side exponent `1 - t / g` stays positive (footnote 4). -/
structure Params where
  t : ℝ
  g : ℝ
  t_pos : 0 < t
  g_pos : 0 < g
  g_le_one : g ≤ 1
  t_lt_g : t < g

/-- Exponent used when the trader buys fyToken: `1 - g t` (paper eq. 20). -/
def aBuy : ℝ := 1 - p.g * p.t

/-- Exponent used when the trader sells fyToken: `1 - t / g` (paper eq. 20, footnote). -/
def aSell : ℝ := 1 - p.t / p.g

The definitions of aBuy and aSell sit inside the namespace Params, where p stands for a value of type Params; p.t and p.g are its time and fee parameter. The fields t_pos, g_pos, g_le_one and t_lt_g are proofs, carried along with the numbers. Every value p : Params therefore comes with the facts 0<t<g≤1, and lemmas such as p.aSell_pos (0<1−t/g) are proved from them. Setting g=1 gives the fee-free pool, Params.noFee.

4.4Price and rate

YieldSpace/Defs.leandefinitions
/-- Marginal price of fyToken in base, `(x / y) ^ t` (reciprocal of paper eq. 13). -/
def price (t x y : ℝ) : ℝ := (x / y) ^ t

/-- Implied rate to maturity, `(y / x) ^ t - 1` (= `1 / price - 1`). -/
def rate (t x y : ℝ) : ℝ := (y / x) ^ t - 1

/-- The paper's interest rate `y / x - 1` (eqs. 2, 11): the rate per unit of scaled time. -/
def paperRate (x y : ℝ) : ℝ := y / x - 1

The relation between the two rates, 1+rate=(1+r)t, is a one-line lemma:

YieldSpace/Rates.leanstatement and proof
/-- How the two rates relate: `1 + rate = (1 + paperRate) ^ t`. The paper's `r` is the
rate per unit of scaled time; `rate` compounds it over the time to maturity. -/
theorem one_add_rate (t x y : ℝ) : 1 + rate t x y = (1 + paperRate x y) ^ t := by
  simp [rate, paperRate]

5The proofs

5.1Non-negative rates (Theorem 1)

A fyToken should not cost more than the base it pays out, since that would mean a negative interest rate. The paper's pool enforces this by checking at the end of each trade that the fyToken price is not above 1, “or, equivalently, that the fyDai reserves are greater than the Dai reserves” (paper, §6.3). Theorem 1 is the direction of that equivalence the check relies on.

Theorem 1 (Non-negative rates). If 0<x≤y and t≥0, then the price (x/y)t is at most 1, and the rates (4) and (5) are non-negative.
Proof. Since 0<x/y≤1, and a number in [0,1] raised to a non-negative power stays in [0,1], we get p=(x/y)t≤1. Then 1/p−1≥0, and r=y/x−1≥0 because y/x≥1. □

The Lean proof of the price statement was shown in Section 3. The two rate statements are rate_nonneg and paperRate_nonneg.

5.2Well-defined trades (Theorem 4)

A trade is well defined if exactly one outcome preserves the invariant, and the pool still holds a positive amount of each token afterwards. Before proving this we need to know which trade sizes are possible.

Trades with a fixed output. Taking Δ out of the y reserve is possible exactly when 0≤Δ<y. Then (y−Δ)a≤ya, so the quantity inside (9) satisfies

k−(y−Δ)a≥k−ya=xa>0.

The new x reserve exists, it is positive, and it is at least x, so the trader pays a non-negative amount.

Trades with a fixed input. Here there is a limit that the constant product does not have. Setting x=0 in xa+ya=k shows that the curve meets the y axis at y=k1/a, as in Figure 1. At that point the pool has paid out all of its base, and a trader who sends in more fyToken has nothing left to receive. For the running pool, k1/a=20.4882=419.76, so a single sale can bring in at most 309.76 fyToken. The exact condition for a sale of Δ is

(y+Δ)a<k,(10)

which the project calls Valid.

YieldSpace/Trades.leandefinition
/-- Exact domain of an input-specified trade. -/
def Valid (a x y Δ : ℝ) : Prop := (y + Δ) ^ a < inv a x y

A simpler sufficient condition is that the trader sends no more than the pool's reserve of the other token, Δ≤x. It follows from the strict subadditivity of z↦za when 0<a<1:

(x+y)a<xa+ya(x,y>0).(11)

To prove (11), let s=x+y. Since 0<x/s<1 and a<1, we have (x/s)a>x/s, that is, xa>(x/s)sa. In the same way ya>(y/s)sa. Adding the two inequalities gives xa+ya>sa. Then, if Δ≤x,

(y+Δ)a≤(y+x)a<xa+ya=k.

For the running pool this guarantees that sales of up to 100 fyToken are possible, while the true limit is 309.76. The bound becomes exact as t→0, where the pool trades one for one and can pay out at most x.

YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement and proof
/-- Strict subadditivity of `z ↦ z ^ a` for `0 < a < 1`. -/
lemma rpow_add_lt (_ha0 : 0 < a) (ha1 : a < 1) {x y : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) (hy : 0 < y) :
    (x + y) ^ a < x ^ a + y ^ a := by
  have hs : 0 < x + y := add_pos hx hy
  have key : ∀ {u : ℝ}, 0 < u → u < x + y → u / (x + y) * (x + y) ^ a < u ^ a := by
    intro u hu hus
    have h0 : 0 < u / (x + y) := div_pos hu hs
    have h1 : u / (x + y) < 1 := (div_lt_one hs).2 hus
    have : (u / (x + y)) ^ (1 : ℝ) < (u / (x + y)) ^ a :=
      (rpow_lt_rpow_left_iff_of_base_lt_one h0 h1).2 ha1
    rw [rpow_one, div_rpow hu.le hs.le, lt_div_iff₀ (rpow_pos_of_pos hs _)] at this
    exact this
  have h1 := key hx (by linarith)
  have h2 := key hy (by linarith)
  have : x / (x + y) * (x + y) ^ a + y / (x + y) * (x + y) ^ a = (x + y) ^ a := by
    rw [← add_mul, ← add_div, div_self hs.ne', one_mul]
  linarith
YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement and proof
/-- An input of at most the opposite reserve is always valid. -/
lemma valid_of_le (ha0 : 0 < a) (ha1 : a < 1) {x y Δ : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) (hy : 0 < y)
    (hΔ0 : 0 ≤ Δ) (hΔx : Δ ≤ x) : Valid a x y Δ := by
  unfold Valid inv
  calc (y + Δ) ^ a ≤ (x + y) ^ a := rpow_le_rpow (by linarith) (by linarith) ha0.le
    _ < x ^ a + y ^ a := rpow_add_lt ha0 ha1 hx hy

The Lean proof of (11) follows the argument above. The local fact key is the inequality xa>(x/s)sa, proved once for any u with 0<u<s, and then used for u=x and u=y.

Theorem 4 (Well-defined trades). Let 0<a<1 and x,y>0.
  1. If Δ≥0 and (10) holds, the payout (8) is non-negative, the new base reserve is positive, and the new reserves lie on the same curve. Any other payout that leaves a non-negative base reserve on the curve is equal to (8).
  2. If 0≤Δ<y, the cost (9) is non-negative, both new reserves are positive, and the new reserves lie on the same curve. Any other cost that leaves a non-negative base reserve on the curve is equal to (9).
Proof. Existence and positivity were shown above, and solve_rpow shows that the new reserves lie on the curve. For (a), the payout is non-negative because (y+Δ)a≥ya, so (k−(y+Δ)a)1/a≤(k−ya)1/a=x. Uniqueness in both parts is eq_solve: a non-negative reserve on the curve must equal (7). □

Uniqueness holds among outcomes that leave a non-negative reserve. Without that restriction the statement would involve Mathlib's values of xa for negative x (Section 3), which have no meaning here.

YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement
/-- **Theorem 4 (input-specified).** For a valid input `Δ ≥ 0` the output lies in `[0, x)`,
so the new reserve is positive, and the invariant is preserved. -/
theorem outGivenIn_spec (ha : 0 < a) {x y Δ : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) (hy : 0 ≤ y) (hΔ : 0 ≤ Δ)
    (hv : Valid a x y Δ) :
    0 ≤ outGivenIn a x y Δ ∧ 0 < x - outGivenIn a x y Δ ∧
      inv a (x - outGivenIn a x y Δ) (y + Δ) = inv a x y := …
YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement and proof
/-- **Theorem 4 (input-specified), uniqueness.** Any trade output that keeps the new
reserve non-negative and preserves the invariant equals `outGivenIn`. -/
theorem outGivenIn_unique (ha : 0 < a) {x y Δ d : ℝ} (hd : 0 ≤ x - d)
    (h : inv a (x - d) (y + Δ) = inv a x y) : d = outGivenIn a x y Δ := by
  have := eq_solve ha hd h
  unfold outGivenIn; linarith
YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement
/-- **Theorem 4 (output-specified).** For `0 ≤ Δ < y` the required input is
non-negative, the reserves stay positive, and the invariant is preserved. -/
theorem inGivenOut_spec (ha : 0 < a) {x y Δ : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) (hΔ : 0 ≤ Δ) (hΔy : Δ < y) :
    0 ≤ inGivenOut a x y Δ ∧ 0 < x + inGivenOut a x y Δ ∧ 0 < y - Δ ∧
      inv a (x + inGivenOut a x y Δ) (y - Δ) = inv a x y := …

5.3Monotonicity (Theorem 2)

Buying fyToken from the pool should make it more expensive, and selling fyToken to the pool should make it cheaper.

Theorem 2 (Monotonicity). Let t>0. A trade that buys a positive amount of fyToken strictly raises the price (x/y)t, and a trade that sells a positive amount strictly lowers it. This holds for each of the four trades in Table 3, on any of the curves.
Proof. Buying fyToken increases x and decreases y, so x/y increases, and b↦bt is strictly increasing on [0,∞) when t>0. Selling does the opposite. It remains to know that a trade of positive size really moves both reserves in those directions, and keeps them positive. That is Theorem 4, together with the lemmas outGivenIn_pos and inGivenOut_pos, which say that a trade of positive size changes both reserves. □

The price in Theorem 2 is the fee-free marginal price (x/y)t, while the trade itself may use any of the curves. The fee-adjusted marginal prices (x/y)gt and (x/y)t/g are also increasing in x/y, so the same argument applies to them.

YieldSpace/Monotone.leanstatement and proof
lemma price_lt_price {t x y x' y' : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) (hx : 0 < x) (hy' : 0 < y')
    (hxx : x ≤ x') (hyy : y' < y) : price t x y < price t x' y' := by
  have hy : 0 < y := hy'.trans hyy
  have : x / y < x' / y' := by
    rw [div_lt_div_iff₀ hy hy']; nlinarith
  exact rpow_lt_rpow (div_nonneg hx.le hy.le) this ht

/-- **Theorem 2.** Buying `Δ > 0` fyToken (output-specified) strictly raises its price. -/
theorem price_lt_after_buyFY (ha : 0 < a) {t x y Δ : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) (hx : 0 < x)
    (hΔ : 0 < Δ) (hΔy : Δ < y) :
    price t x y < price t (x + inGivenOut a x y Δ) (y - Δ) :=
  price_lt_price ht hx (by linarith) (by linarith [(inGivenOut_spec ha hx hΔ.le hΔy).1])
    (by linarith)

In price_lt_after_buyFY, the term (inGivenOut_spec ha hx hΔ.le hΔy).1 takes the first part of Theorem 4, that the cost is non-negative. hΔ.le turns 0<Δ into 0≤Δ.

5.4Path independence (Theorem 6)

The invariant is recomputed from the reserves before every trade. One might therefore expect that splitting a trade into pieces changes the result. It does not. The first piece ends on the curve it started on, so the second piece computes the same k.

Theorem 6 (Path independence). Let 0<a<1 and Δ1​,Δ2​≥0, and suppose the combined sale is possible: (y+Δ1​+Δ2​)a≤k. Selling Δ1​ and then Δ2​ pays the same total as selling Δ1​+Δ2​ at once. The same holds for trades with a fixed output, when Δ1​≤y.
Proof. Let x1​=(k−(y+Δ1​)a)1/a be the base reserve after the first sale. Then x1a​+(y+Δ1​)a=k, so the second sale computes the same invariant k and leaves the base reserve at x2​=(k−(y+Δ1​+Δ2​)a)1/a. The total paid is (x−x1​)+(x1​−x2​)=x−x2​, which is (8) for a single sale of Δ1​+Δ2​. □

In the running pool, selling 4 fyToken pays 3.744 base, and selling 6 more then pays 5.366. The total, 9.110, is the payout for selling 10 at once.

Since the proof works for any exponent a, path independence also holds on the fee curves, as long as the pieces go in the same direction. The paper points this out as an advantage over fees charged as a percentage of the amount sent in, as in Uniswap, where splitting a trade changes the total fee (paper, end of §5). Pieces in opposite directions use different curves. That is the round trip of Section 5.8.

YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement and proof
/-- **Theorem 6 (input-specified).** -/
theorem outGivenIn_add (ha : 0 < a) {x y Δ₁ Δ₂ : ℝ} (hy : 0 ≤ y) (h₁ : 0 ≤ Δ₁) (h₂ : 0 ≤ Δ₂)
    (hv : (y + (Δ₁ + Δ₂)) ^ a ≤ inv a x y) :
    outGivenIn a x y (Δ₁ + Δ₂) =
      outGivenIn a x y Δ₁ + outGivenIn a (x - outGivenIn a x y Δ₁) (y + Δ₁) Δ₂ := by
  have hk : 0 ≤ inv a x y - (y + Δ₁) ^ a := by
    have : (y + Δ₁) ^ a ≤ (y + (Δ₁ + Δ₂)) ^ a := rpow_le_rpow (by linarith) (by linarith) ha.le
    linarith
  have hx1 : x - outGivenIn a x y Δ₁ = solve a (inv a x y) (y + Δ₁) := by
    unfold outGivenIn; ring
  rw [hx1]
  unfold outGivenIn
  rw [inv_solve ha hk, add_assoc]
  ring

The Lean proof follows the informal one. hk shows that the intermediate reserves are valid, hx1 names the intermediate base reserve, and the rewrite rw [inv_solve ha hk] is the step “the second sale computes the same k”.

5.5Scale invariance (Theorem 8)

Suppose every reserve is multiplied by λ>0, as happens when liquidity is added in proportion to the existing reserves. The invariant does not scale by λ:

(λx)a+(λy)a=λa(xa+ya)=λ1−tk.

Trades still scale in the simplest possible way, provided the trade size scales too.

Theorem 8 (Scale invariance). Let λ>0. Multiplying both reserves and the trade size by λ multiplies the result of every trade by λ, for trades with a fixed input (when they are possible) and with a fixed output. The price and the rate do not change.
Proof. In (7), (λak−(λz)a)1/a=(λa(k−za))1/a=λ(k−za)1/a. So every reserve after the scaled trade is λ times the corresponding reserve after the original trade, and so is the difference between the reserves before and after. The price depends only on λx/λy=x/y. □

A pool with reserves (1000,1100) pays 91.10 base for 100 fyToken, ten times the 9.110 that the pool (100,110) pays for 10. If only the reserves are scaled and the trade size stays fixed, there is no relation this simple.

YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement and proof
theorem inv_smul {l x y : ℝ} (hl : 0 ≤ l) (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hy : 0 ≤ y) :
    inv a (l * x) (l * y) = l ^ a * inv a x y := by
  simp [inv, mul_rpow hl hx, mul_rpow hl hy, mul_add]

lemma solve_smul (ha : 0 < a) {l k z : ℝ} (hl : 0 ≤ l) (hz : 0 ≤ z) (h : 0 ≤ k - z ^ a) :
    solve a (l ^ a * k) (l * z) = l * solve a k z := by
  unfold solve
  rw [mul_rpow hl hz, ← mul_sub, mul_rpow (rpow_nonneg hl _) h, rpow_rpow_inv hl ha.ne']
YieldSpace/Trades.leanstatement
/-- **Theorem 8 (input-specified).** -/
theorem outGivenIn_smul (ha : 0 < a) {l x y Δ : ℝ} (hl : 0 ≤ l) (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hy : 0 ≤ y)
    (hΔ : 0 ≤ Δ) (hv : (y + Δ) ^ a ≤ inv a x y) :
    outGivenIn a (l * x) (l * y) (l * Δ) = l * outGivenIn a x y Δ := …

The hypothesis hv keeps k−(y+Δ)a non-negative. It is needed because the step (λac)1/a=λc1/a, Mathlib's mul_rpow, requires both factors to be non-negative.

5.6A change of variables

The remaining proofs about prices use one idea twice. Write

u=xa,w=ya.

In these variables the invariant u+w=k is a straight line, and every trade moves along it. If a trade raises w by d, it lowers u by exactly d. This is the step at the heart of the paper's derivation in Appendix C, where integrating y−tdy=−x−tdx says that y1−t and x1−t change by equal and opposite amounts. The reserves themselves are recovered with

ψ(s)=s1/a,

which is increasing and, because 1/a>1, strictly convex. A sale of Δ fyToken is therefore described by two intervals of the same width d: the base interval [u′,u], which u moves across, and the fyToken interval [w,w′], which w moves across. The amounts that change hands are the increases of ψ across them:

out=ψ(u)−ψ(u′),Δ=ψ(w′)−ψ(w).(12)

In the running example a=1/2 and ψ(s)=s2. Selling 10 fyToken moves w from 110​=10.488 to 120​=10.954, so d=0.466, and moves u from 10 down to 9.534. Then Δ=10.9542−10.4882=10 and out=102−9.5342=9.110.

Because ψ is convex, its increase over an interval of fixed width is larger the further right the interval lies. In Figure 2 the base interval lies to the left of the fyToken interval, because x<y, and so the trader receives less base than the fyToken they send. The next two sections make this precise.

5.7Price impact (Theorem 7)

The average price of a trade is the amount of base exchanged per fyToken, out/Δ for a sale. The difference between the average price and the marginal price before the trade is the trade's price impact. We want to show that price impact always works against the trader, and grows with the size of the trade. In the running example, selling 10 fyToken happens at an average price of 0.911. That lies between the marginal price before the trade, 0.9535, and the marginal price after it, (90.890/120)0.5=0.870. Figure 3 shows the same fact on the curve, for a larger sale.

Theorem 7 (Price impact). Let 0<a<1 and τ=1−a, let x,y,Δ>0, let the sale of Δ be possible, and let out be its payout (8). Then (y+Δx−out​)τ<Δout​<(yx​)τ. For a purchase of Δ<y the average price likewise lies strictly between the marginal price before the trade (now the lower bound) and the marginal price after it. The average price of a sale strictly decreases as the sale grows, and the average price of a purchase strictly increases.

Proof. Use the variables of Section 5.6. By the mean value theorem there are ξ∈(u′,u) and η∈(w,w′) with

ψ(u)−ψ(u′)=ψ′(ξ)d,ψ(w′)−ψ(w)=ψ′(η)d.

Since ψ′(s)=a1​s1/a−1, dividing the first equation by the second and using (12) gives

Δout​=(ηξ​)1/a−1.(13)

The marginal prices can be written in the same variables. Since x=u1/a, y=w1/a and τ/a=1/a−1,

(yx​)τ=(wu​)1/a−1,

and likewise the marginal price after the trade is (u′/w′)1/a−1. Now u′<ξ<u and w<η<w′ give

w′u′​<ηξ​<wu​,

and raising to the positive power 1/a−1 gives the inequalities for a sale.

A purchase is a sale run backwards. Buying Δ from (x,y) ends at (x+in,y−Δ), and selling Δ from there returns to (x,y) and pays exactly in (the lemma outGivenIn_reverse). Applying the result for sales at the later reserves gives the result for purchases.

For the last claim, take 0<Δ1​<Δ2​, and use Theorem 6 to split the larger sale into Δ1​ followed by Δ2​−Δ1​. The second piece starts where the first one ends. By what we just proved, its average price is below the marginal price at that point, which is below the average price of the first piece. The average price of the whole sale is a weighted average of the two pieces' average prices, so it is below that of the first piece alone. The argument for purchases is the same. □

For a purchase from the running pool the order is reversed. Buying 5 fyToken costs 4.881 base, an average price of 0.976, between 0.9535 before the trade and 0.999 after it.

Mathlib's mean value theorem, exists_hasDerivAt_eq_slope, needs the function to be continuous on the closed interval and differentiable inside it. The lemma hasDerivAt_rpow_const supplies the derivative pzp−1 of z↦zp.

YieldSpace/PriceImpact.leanstatement and proof
lemma mvt_rpow {p u v : ℝ} (hp : 0 ≤ p) (hu : 0 < u) (huv : u < v) :
    ∃ ξ ∈ Ioo u v, v ^ p - u ^ p = p * ξ ^ (p - 1) * (v - u) := by
  obtain ⟨ξ, hξ, h⟩ := exists_hasDerivAt_eq_slope (fun z : ℝ => z ^ p)
    (fun z => p * z ^ (p - 1)) huv
    (fun z _ => (continuousAt_rpow_const z p (Or.inr hp)).continuousWithinAt)
    (fun z hz => hasDerivAt_rpow_const (Or.inl (hu.trans hz.1).ne'))
  refine ⟨ξ, hξ, ?_⟩
  rw [h, div_mul_cancel₀ _ (sub_pos.2 huv).ne']

`post price < average price < pre price`. -/

On the fee curves, τ is gt or t/g, so the prices that bracket the average are the fee-adjusted marginal prices. The fee-free versions, avgPrice_sellFY_noFee and avgPrice_buyFY_noFee, state the result with price t.

5.8Round trips (Theorem 3)

Suppose a trader sells Δ fyToken and then immediately buys Δ fyToken back. Without a fee both trades use the same curve, and the trader should end where they started. With a fee, the sale uses the curve with exponent α=1−t/g, which we call the α-curve, and the purchase uses the curve with exponent β=1−gt, the β-curve. When g<1, α<β. We want the fee to make every round trip cost the trader something.

Theorem 3 (No free round trips).
  1. Without a fee, a round trip breaks even: buying Δ back costs exactly what selling Δ paid.
  2. Let g<1, 0<x≤y and Δ>0, and let the sale be possible. Then buying Δ back costs strictly more than selling Δ paid.

Part (b) needs the hypothesis x≤y, and without it the statement is false. We return to this after the proof.

Proof. (a) The sale leaves reserves (x1​,y+Δ) on the curve through (x,y). Buying Δ back on the same curve leads to the point of that curve with fyToken reserve y, and by the uniqueness in Theorem 4 that point is (x,y). So the purchase costs x−x1​, which is what the sale paid.

(b) The sale leaves reserves (x1​,y+Δ) on the α-curve. Use the variables of Section 5.6 with the exponent α:

u′=x1α​,u=xα,w=yα,w′=(y+Δ)α.

As before, [u′,u] and [w,w′] have the same width. The purchase uses the β-curve through (x1​,y+Δ), and ends at a point (x2​,y) with x2β​+yβ=x1β​+(y+Δ)β. It costs x2​−x1​, and the sale paid x−x1​, so the purchase costs more exactly when x2​>x. Raising both sides to the power β and substituting for x2β​,

x2​>x⟺x1β​+(y+Δ)β−yβ>xβ⟺xβ−x1β​<(y+Δ)β−yβ.(14)

Write each β-power through an α-power, zβ=(zα)β/α, and let φ(s)=sβ/α. Then (14) reads

φ(u)−φ(u′)<φ(w′)−φ(w).

Since β/α>1, φ is strictly convex, so its increase over an interval of fixed width grows as the interval moves right. The two intervals have the same width, and u′<u≤w because x1​<x≤y. So the inequality holds. □

In the running pool with g=0.95, selling 10 fyToken pays 9.066 base and buying 10 back costs 9.155. The trader loses 0.089.

Where the hypothesis comes from. The argument used only that the base interval [u′,u] lies to the left of the fyToken interval [w,w′], that is, x1​<y. If instead x1​>y, the base interval lies to the right, the inequality reverses, and the round trip pays the trader. When x1​=y the two intervals coincide and the round trip breaks even. Figure 5 shows this for y=100, Δ=10, t=0.5 and g=0.95. The trader's result changes sign at exactly x=110, where the sale leaves x1​=100=y. For example, starting from (x,y)=(200,100) the sale pays 13.782 and buying back costs 13.351, a gain of 0.431.

This agrees with a remark in the paper (Appendix E): when the interest rate is negative, that is, x>y, the fee benefits the trader rather than the pool. The paper notes that such reserves can arise if someone sends base tokens directly to the pool. The Lean theorem assumes x≤y, which implies x1​<y. Only this direction is formalized.

The convexity step uses Mathlib's StrictConvexOn.slope_strict_mono_adjacent: for a strictly convex function and points p<q<r, the slope over [p,q] is less than the slope over [q,r]. When the intervals touch (u=w) one application suffices. When they are apart, two applications compare [u′,u] with [u,w], and then [u,w] with [w,w′].

YieldSpace/Monotone.leanstatement and proof
/-- **Theorem 3 (no fee).** Selling `Δ` Y and buying `Δ` Y back on the same curve is
exactly break-even. -/
theorem roundTrip_eq (ha : 0 < a) {x y Δ : ℝ} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hk : (y + Δ) ^ a ≤ inv a x y) :
    inGivenOut a (x - outGivenIn a x y Δ) (y + Δ) Δ = outGivenIn a x y Δ := by
  rw [sub_outGivenIn]
  unfold inGivenOut
  rw [inv_solve ha (by linarith), add_sub_cancel_right, solve_inv_self ha hx]
  unfold outGivenIn; ring
YieldSpace/Monotone.leanstatement and proof
/-- Same-length increments of a strictly convex function grow strictly when the interval
moves right (here `v ≤ w`, so the intervals do not overlap). -/
lemma increment_lt {φ : ℝ → ℝ} (hφ : StrictConvexOn ℝ (Set.Ici 0) φ) {u v w w' : ℝ}
    (hu : 0 ≤ u) (huv : u < v) (hvw : v ≤ w) (hlen : w' - w = v - u) :
    φ v - φ u < φ w' - φ w := by
  have hd : 0 < v - u := by linarith
  have hmem : ∀ {z}, u ≤ z → z ∈ Set.Ici (0 : ℝ) := fun h => Set.mem_Ici.2 (hu.trans h)
  have key : (φ v - φ u) / (v - u) < (φ w' - φ w) / (w' - w) := by
    rcases hvw.eq_or_lt with h | h
    · subst h
      exact hφ.slope_strict_mono_adjacent (hmem le_rfl) (hmem (by linarith)) huv (by linarith)
    · calc (φ v - φ u) / (v - u) < (φ w - φ v) / (w - v) :=
            hφ.slope_strict_mono_adjacent (hmem le_rfl) (hmem (by linarith)) huv h
        _ < (φ w' - φ w) / (w' - w) :=
            hφ.slope_strict_mono_adjacent (hmem huv.le) (hmem (by linarith)) h (by linarith)
  rw [hlen] at key
  exact (div_lt_div_iff_of_pos_right hd).1 key
YieldSpace/Monotone.leanstatement and proof
/-- **Theorem 3 (core).** Sell `Δ` Y on the flatter curve `α`, then buy `Δ` back on the
steeper curve `β > α`: the buy-back costs strictly more X than the sale paid, **provided
`x ≤ y`** (non-negative rates). Without that hypothesis the claim is false; see README. -/
theorem roundTrip_lt {α β : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hαβ : α < β) {x y Δ : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x)
    (hxy : x ≤ y) (hΔ : 0 < Δ) (hv : Valid α x y Δ) :
    outGivenIn α x y Δ < inGivenOut β (x - outGivenIn α x y Δ) (y + Δ) Δ := by
  have hβ : 0 < β := hα.trans hαβ
  have hy : 0 < y := hx.trans_le hxy
  obtain ⟨-, hx1pos, hinv⟩ := outGivenIn_spec hα hx hy.le hΔ.le hv
  set x1 := x - outGivenIn α x y Δ with hx1def
  have hx1lt : x1 < x := by linarith [outGivenIn_pos hα hx hy.le hΔ hv]
  -- move to `α`-power coordinates and use convexity of `z ↦ z ^ (β / α)`
  have hconv : StrictConvexOn ℝ (Set.Ici 0) (fun z : ℝ => z ^ (β / α)) :=
    strictConvexOn_rpow ((one_lt_div hα).2 hαβ)
  have hpow : ∀ {z : ℝ}, 0 ≤ z → (z ^ α) ^ (β / α) = z ^ β := by
    intro z hz
    rw [← rpow_mul hz, mul_div_cancel₀ _ hα.ne']
  have hlen : (y + Δ) ^ α - y ^ α = x ^ α - x1 ^ α := by
    unfold inv at hinv; linarith
  have hinc := increment_lt hconv (rpow_nonneg hx1pos.le α)
    (rpow_lt_rpow hx1pos.le hx1lt hα) (rpow_le_rpow hx.le hxy hα.le) hlen
  simp only [hpow hx.le, hpow hx1pos.le, hpow hy.le, hpow (by linarith : (0 : ℝ) ≤ y + Δ)]
    at hinc
  -- `x` is strictly below the X-reserve that the buy-back curve requires
  have hlt : x < solve β (inv β x1 (y + Δ)) y := by
    have h0 : 0 ≤ x ^ β := rpow_nonneg hx.le β
    have : x ^ β < inv β x1 (y + Δ) - y ^ β := by unfold inv; linarith
    have := rpow_lt_rpow h0 this (inv_pos.2 hβ)
    rwa [rpow_rpow_inv hx.le hβ.ne'] at this
  unfold inGivenOut
  rw [add_sub_cancel_right]
  have : outGivenIn α x y Δ = x - x1 := by rw [hx1def]; ring
  linarith

In roundTrip_lt, hconv is the convexity of φ, hpow is the identity (zα)β/α=zβ, hlen says the two intervals have the same width, and hinc is (14), obtained from increment_lt and rewritten with hpow. hlt is the statement x<x2​. The theorem about the fee trades is then a direct application:

YieldSpace/Monotone.leanstatement and proof
/-- **Theorem 3 (fees, fyToken round trip).** Sell `Δ` fyToken, then buy `Δ` fyToken
back: with a real fee (`g < 1`) and `x ≤ y`, the trader strictly loses base. -/
theorem Params.roundTrip_loss (p : Params) (hg : p.g < 1) {x y Δ : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x)
    (hxy : x ≤ y) (hΔ : 0 < Δ) (hv : Valid p.aSell x y Δ) :
    p.sellFYToken x y Δ < p.buyFYToken (x - p.sellFYToken x y Δ) (y + Δ) Δ :=
  roundTrip_lt p.aSell_pos (p.aSell_lt_aBuy hg) hx hxy hΔ hv

5.9Convergence at maturity (Theorem 5)

At maturity a fyToken is worth exactly one unit of base, so the pool should trade one for one. Every exponent in use, 1−t, 1−gt and 1−t/g, tends to 1 as t→0, and at exponent 1 the invariant is the constant sum x+y=k.

Theorem 5 (Convergence at maturity). Fix reserves x,y and a trade size Δ. As t→0:
  1. for each z, the point of the curve through (x,y) with fyToken reserve z has a base reserve that tends to x+y−z, the value on the constant-sum line;
  2. the result of each of the four trades in Table 3 tends to Δ;
  3. the price (x/y)t tends to 1.
Proof. For (a) it suffices to show that a↦(xa+ya−za)1/a is continuous at a=1, because then its limit is its value there, x+y−z. Each a↦ca is continuous at a=1, so is a↦1/a, and (b,e)↦be is continuous at every point where e>0. At a=1 the exponent 1/a is 1, so the pieces combine. Each trade result is x minus such a value, or such a value minus x, which gives (b). For (c), t↦(x/y)t is continuous and equals 1 at t=0. □

In Mathlib, limits are written with filters. Tendsto f (𝓝 1) (𝓝 L) means that f(a)→L as a→1, where 𝓝 1 stands for the neighborhoods of 1. The project proves continuity in the exponent once, and then composes it with any path of exponents e that tends to 1, along any filter l. The same lemma therefore gives the fee-free result and the results with fees.

at `a = 1`, where it equals the constant-sum value `x₀ + y₀ - z`. -/
theorem tendsto_solve_one (x₀ y₀ z : ℝ) :
    Tendsto (fun a => solve a (inv a x₀ y₀) z) (𝓝 1) (𝓝 (x₀ + y₀ - z)) := by
  have hc : ∀ b : ℝ, ContinuousAt (fun a : ℝ => b ^ a) 1 := fun b =>
    continuousAt_const.rpow continuousAt_id (Or.inr one_pos)
  have hcont : ContinuousAt (fun a => solve a (inv a x₀ y₀) z) 1 := by
    unfold solve inv
    exact (((hc x₀).add (hc y₀)).sub (hc z)).rpow (continuousAt_id.inv₀ one_ne_zero)
      (Or.inr (by simp))
  simpa [solve, inv] using hcont.tendsto

pointwise to the constant-sum line `x + y = x₀ + y₀`. -/

    (x₀ y₀ z : ℝ) :
    Tendsto (fun i => solve (e i) (inv (e i) x₀ y₀) z) l (𝓝 (x₀ + y₀ - z)) := …

/-- **Theorem 5 (with fees).** For a fixed fee parameter `g`, all four fee trades become
1:1 as `t → 0`. -/
theorem tendsto_feeTrades (g x y Δ : ℝ) :
    Tendsto (fun t => outGivenIn (1 - t / g) x y Δ) (𝓝 0) (𝓝 Δ) ∧
    Tendsto (fun t => inGivenOut (1 - g * t) x y Δ) (𝓝 0) (𝓝 Δ) ∧
    Tendsto (fun t => outGivenIn (1 - g * t) y x Δ) (𝓝 0) (𝓝 Δ) ∧
    Tendsto (fun t => inGivenOut (1 - t / g) y x Δ) (𝓝 0) (𝓝 Δ) := …

Mathlib's lemma ContinuousAt.rpow requires either a nonzero base or a positive exponent. At a=1 the exponent is positive, so no hypothesis on the reserves is needed. The convergence is pointwise: it holds for each fixed trade, and is not claimed to be uniform over all trades.

6Where the formalization and the paper differ

Writing each property precisely enough for Lean to check it raised the following points.

Two notions of rate

The paper's rate, r=y/x−1 in (5), is a rate per unit of scaled time; with t=1 at four years it is a four-year rate. The return to maturity, (y/x)t−1 in (4), is a different number. Both are defined in the project, and one_add_rate relates them.

Round trips at negative rates

“A round trip with a fee loses money” holds when x≤y, and fails when the sale leaves more base than the pool's starting fyToken (Section 5.8, Figure 5). The paper mentions this for negative rates in Appendix E. Theorem 3 carries the hypothesis x≤y.

A limit on trades with a fixed input

The constant power sum curve meets both axes, so a sale of fyToken is possible only while (y+Δ)1−t<k (Section 5.2). The constant product has no such limit, and the paper does not discuss it. A sale of at most x fyToken is always possible.

The worked example in §6.3

The paper's example sells 100 fyDai into a pool with 100 Dai and 100 virtual fyDai, at t=0.5 with g=0.95, and reports x=34.31, so that 65.69 Dai is paid out. That is the result on the fee-free curve, exponent 0.5. On the selling curve the text describes, exponent 1−t/g=0.4737, the base reserve becomes 35.39 and the payout is 64.61 Dai.

Path independence with fees

The paper's remark that splitting a trade does not change the fee paid (end of §5) is proved here (Theorem 6) for pieces in the same direction. Pieces in opposite directions form a round trip, which is covered by Theorem 3.

Which curve each trade uses

The paper assigns curves by direction, buying or selling fyToken. Table 3 extends this to trades where the trader fixes the amount of base.

What is not formalized

Liquidity tokens and the accounting for virtual reserves (paper §6), the proofs about the share invariant (Appendices E and F), and the limit t→1 (Appendix D). In this project y is simply the fyToken reserve used in the formula, virtual reserves included.

ABuilding the project

The source is at github.com/aniemerg/yieldspace-lean. Checking the proofs needs elan, Lean's toolchain manager; Mathlib's compiled files are downloaded rather than built locally. Rebuilding this page also needs Python 3 and Node.js.

git clone https://github.com/aniemerg/yieldspace-lean.git && cd yieldspace-lean
lake exe cache get             # download compiled Mathlib
lake build                     # check every proof
lake env lean AxiomCheck.lean  # list the axioms behind each main theorem
(cd site && npm install)       # KaTeX, used to typeset the mathematics
python3 site/build.py          # rebuild this page into site/dist/
